results.content:
Google Japan has looked at the conventional keyboard and decided that perhaps our fingers have been doing too much of the work. Developed by the Gboard team, the new Gboard Kurukuru Version places its keys on moving conveyor belts, allowing characters to travel toward the user rather than asking the user to reach across a fixed layout. The experimental device turns one of the most familiar tools on a desk into something closer to a miniature production line, with typing becoming a matter of catching the right character as it rolls into place. [...] Kurukuru arrives as the 15th entry in Google Japan’s long-running series of unconventional Gboard experiments. Previous editions have stretched the keyboard into a single elongated row, twisted it into a double-sided loop and, in 2025, replaced traditional typing with rotary telephone-style dials. The latest version continues that habit of taking an everyday interface far too literally, then engineering it seriously enough to work. Google is also considering color variations, a high-speed mode and longer or more portable short versions, although none have been announced as commercial products.

# Google Unveils A Physical Gboard On Conveyor Belts

By Paulo Montenegro, on 10/09/2026 07:50 PDT

Google Japan has introduced its latest experimental hardware interface, the Gboard Kurukuru Version, a concept peripheral that reverses standard typing mechanics by placing individual keys on motorized conveyor belts. Rather than requiring hands to travel across a static surface, the device continuously transports characters directly to the user’s fingertips. [...] The hardware architecture relies on four continuous belts, each carrying 29 switches for a total of 116 keys. As the mechanical tracks rotate, the user keeps their hand relatively stationary, timing input execution as the targeted letter rolls into position. The design supports direct entry of both uppercase and lowercase characters and enables complete navigation using only one hand or a single finger.

This operational layout frees the secondary hand for external desktop tasks, such as navigating a mouse or holding a drink. The Kurukuru marks the 15th iteration in Google Japan’s ongoing series of unconventional input experiments, following earlier releases such as a single elongated linear row, a double-sided loop, and rotary telephone dials.

results.title: The Best Open-Source, Privacy-First Alternatives to Gboard | Lifehacker
results.content:
In my testing, I found that the FUTO keyboard offers a smoother, more reliable typing experience compared to Gboard. A small example is the spacebar gesture. In Gboard, you can move the cursor by swiping on the spacebar, but it’s a bit confusing for me. You hold it for a split second, and then swipe. In FUTO, swiping on the spacebar instantly moves the cursor, every single time. The downside to being completely private is, of course, that you lose out on cross-device support. Your personal dictionary, or clipboard, can’t sync between all your devices. While Gboard is a more complete package, FUTO's privacy features do make up for that loss.

## HeliBoard is the Gboard alternative for security purists

FUTO Keyboard is designed to be a direct Gboard replacement. It looks like Gboard, and it works like Gboard. But underneath, it’s completely open-source, free, and private. By default, none of your keystrokes leave your device.
